extracted.intended_audience: public-interest advocates, regulatory comment authors, and legal scholars studying notice-and-comment processes
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for drafting effective public-interest regulatory comments (notice-and-comment) drawn from empirical analysis of Volcker Rule submissions; focuses on how non-industry commenters can produce submissions that agencies will find usable and persuasive. Emphasizes legal analysis, empirical evidence, substantive coordination, and matching industry depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the comment include legal analysis citing relevant statutes and authorities?
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the comment include legal analysis citing relevant statutes and authorities?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Krawiec documents that financial-institution comments featured detailed legal arguments relying on numerous statutes and cases. Effective non-industry comments should cite the statute the rule implements and authorities supporting the public-interest reading. Citations to case law, statutory text, and doctrinal authorities increase usability to agency reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the comment include empirical data or evidence?
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the comment include empirical data or evidence?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Industry submissions often included thorough empirical data. Public-interest commenters need empirical evidence as well—not necessarily as much as industry, but sufficient to be credible and to allow agencies/OIRA to rely on it. Data, analysis, and concrete evidence make a submission actionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is the comment substantively distinguished from form-letter content?
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the comment substantively distinguished from form-letter content?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Krawiec found ~7,316 identical brief form letters that lacked data or analysis and were largely useless to decision-makers. Substantive, individualized comments (the ~515 substantive citizen submissions) were the ones that mattered. Avoid generic boilerplate; provide unique, specific arguments and evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the comment engage the legislative history or statutory purpose?
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the comment engage the legislative history or statutory purpose?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Financial-institution comments referenced Dodd-Frank legislative history. Effective public-interest comments should similarly engage legislative history and statutory purpose to support interpretive positions and show how the rule aligns with Congress's intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is the comment part of a coordinated set of substantive public-interest submissions rather than a form-letter campaign?
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the comment part of a coordinated set of substantive public-interest submissions rather than a form-letter campaign?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Krawiec's findings suggest coordinated substantive submissions can outweigh sheer volume of form letters. Building a coalition of well-researched, substantive comments makes public-interest positions more influential than mass form-letter campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the comment match (in some dimension) the analytical depth of likely industry submissions?
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the comment match (in some dimension) the analytical depth of likely industry submissions?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Industry comments were extensive and analytically deep. Public-interest commenters cannot rely on volume alone; they must match industry on length, depth, or other analytical dimensions to be competitive. This may mean more detailed legal argumentation, empirical work, or focused policy analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed legal arguments relying on numerous statutes and cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Financial-institution comments featured detailed legal arguments relying on numerous statutes and cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As an observed success factor for industry submissions, detailed multi-source legal argumentation (statutes, cases, regulations) provides the doctrinal scaffolding agencies use. Public-interest comments should emulate this level of legal rigor when arguing statutory interpretation or regulatory consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to Dodd-Frank legislative history
rubrics_metrics.description: Financial-institution comments referenced Dodd-Frank legislative history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citing legislative history (e.g., committee reports, floor statements) was a specific tactic industry used to support their readings. Where relevant, public-interest comments should marshal legislative-history evidence to bolster interpretive claims about statutory purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough empirical data
rubrics_metrics.description: Industry submissions included thorough empirical data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical work accompanying legal argument made industry submissions more persuasive. Public-interest commenters should provide empirical analysis, data, or citations to credible empirical studies to substantiate claims about effects, costs, or benefits of regulatory choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generally narrow interpretation of the rule's scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally narrow interpretation of the rule's scope was characteristic of industry comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Industry often advanced narrow, focused readings of the rule to limit regulatory impact. Public-interest commenters should consider offering precise, well-supported interpretive positions (even if broader in policy aim) that agencies can operationalize in rule text or guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: Sincerity and volume are not enough
rubrics_metrics.description: Sincerity and volume alone (e.g., 'don't let big banks screw Joe the Plummer') are insufficient to influence agency decisionmaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Krawiec emphasizes that raw frustration, slogans, and high-volume form-letter campaigns are largely unusable by agencies and OIRA. Emotional appeals or mass-signature campaigns without substantive legal or empirical content will likely be ignored.
